doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Katrina and the album's turbulent passages
summary: A reviewer linked the album to Katrina; Jordan says the forces were his fellow musicians and tells of a more powerful Brooklyn club gig.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: That brings me to a question about, you know I think it’s easy to misread the intention of musicians sometimes. Like if you listen to some of the later Coltrane records you might think that John Coltrane was really angry or something like that.
Some people say he was stark raving mad.

But you made a comment regarding this and someone said, I’m reading from the thing, “the album’s turbulent passages almost instinctually call to mind the destructive surge of Katrina.” That was this person’s thought. But you said that you acknowledged that but with a chuckle. “I was contending with the powerful forces all right but they were my compatriots. They were the guys I was playing with.”
Exactly. That’s right. Katrina didn’t have nothing to do with that. I wasn’t even thinking about Katrina. That was all over.
Okay. So it was a musical response.
That’s right, it was a musical response other than that, that’s right. But I’ll tell you one thing, we played a gig before that that they were supposed to give as an extra bonus in

Brooklyn somewhere. It was much more powerful than that because boy we were smoking on that. They were supposed to — maybe they may use it on another record if they can get it because it was in a club and they recorded it in a club. They had, I mean there was one of them knock-out things that William was playing, some of them African instruments in there but it was much more uptempo and out than that.
So when you use the term “knock out drag out” you are talking about really wailing.
